title: A Nation Taken to Court
overview: The LORD brings a case against Judah and Jerusalem, rejecting their worship because they ignore injustice, and offers them a choice between cleansing and ruin.

parts.label: Heaven and earth as witnesses (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: Isaiah spoke during the reigns of four kings in the late 700s BC, and he opens like a court case, calling heaven and earth to listen as Moses once did. God is the parent whose children turned on him, and even an ox knows who feeds it while his people do not know him.

parts.label: A beaten body, a ruined land (vv. 5-9)
parts.note: The nation is pictured as a body covered in untreated wounds, meaning a land burned and stripped by invaders, with Jerusalem left alone like a flimsy watchman's hut in a field. Many scholars link this to an Assyrian invasion, possibly in 701 BC, though the date is uncertain.

parts.label: Worship without justice (vv. 10-17)
parts.note: Calling the leaders Sodom, God says he hates their sacrifices and holy days because the hands raised in prayer are full of blood. The point is not that worship is wrong but that it is empty alongside violence, so he asks instead for justice for orphans and widows, who had no one to protect them.

parts.label: An offer to settle the case (vv. 18-20)
parts.note: God invites the people to talk the matter through, as in a courtroom, and says their sins, stained red like the blood on their hands, can become white as snow. Most read this as an offer of forgiveness tied to the choice that follows, and Christians have also read it as pointing to forgiveness through Jesus.

parts.label: The faithful city corrupted (vv. 21-26)
parts.note: Jerusalem, once known for justice, is pictured as an unfaithful wife, her silver turned to dross (the waste left when metal is refined) and her leaders chasing bribes. God says he will melt out the impurities as in a furnace and restore honest judges, so it can again be called a faithful city.

parts.label: Sacred trees and a coming fire (vv. 27-31)
parts.note: The sacred oaks and gardens were likely places where other gods were worshiped, and those who trusted them will wither like a garden without water. The strong man becomes dry fiber and his own work the spark that burns him, a picture of wrongdoing destroying itself.

think: Where do you see a gap between how people or institutions present themselves and how they treat those with the least power?
